# Introduction
<!--  Situation  --> 
The release of 
Toronto's *Big Move* in 2008 [@Salsberg:2010aa] 
provides an early example of the 'mobility hub' concept, 
in the context of regional transport and landuse planning. 
More recently, 
the ``Shared Mobility Hub" idea has been introduced, 
wherein 
"...emphasis is given on shared mobility options such as bikes, scooters and cars(, while c)onnection with public transport (transit) is desirable but not necessary" [@Roukouni:2023aa]. 
Shared *electric* mobility hubs, 
sometimes called eHUBs [@Bosehans:2023aa], 
add the possibility of on-site recharging 
of micro-mobility vehicles (as well as shared e-cars). 
Along such lines, 
four shared e-mobility hubs have recently been implemented in 
Letterkenny, Galway, Waterford and the suburbs of Dublin, 
as part of the Electric shaRed mOBilityhUbS Trial (ROBUST) project [@ROBUST:2025aa].
Each hub includes 
e-bikes, 
e-cargo bikes, 
and shared electric cars 
as part of the ‘base’ offering, 
as well as power infrastructure to support recharging of these vehicles, 
and other potential future uses [@Atlantic-Technological-University:2025ab, @Atlantic-Technological-University:2025aa, @Waterford-City-and-County-Council:2025aa]. 


<!--  Problem  -->
Shared micromobility, 
including dockless e-bike and e-scooter systems, 
have variously faced challenges, including: 
poor user behaviour with respect to parking; 
a need for workers to re-position vehicles and replace batteries; 
poor build quality of many such vehicles; 
market distortion, including related to 
large fleets in central areas;
and the risk of fires when battery recharging is done using non-bespoke or appropriately designed facilities (e.g. in gig-workers' houses)(see @Zhang:2022aa, @Meigs:2023aa, @Ferguson:2025aa and others).
In contrast, 
at the ROBUST hubs 
there is a dedicated charging 
and parking space for each micro-mobility vehicle, 
which has to be returned to the same hub from which it was hired 
(i.e. A-to-A trips only). 
This may provide 
operational advantages (minimal staffing), 
but also for a more community-based 
service profile 
(with hubs potentially located in small towns 
or outside of city centres) 
so as to help towards 
providing for last-mile and 
and more occasional trips 
that cannot be easily accomplished 
on foot, 
personal bicycle 
or by transit. 
A nearby eHUB might also help 
communities transition to 
electric cars, 
without the large
capital expense 
involved in purchasing a private e-car. 

<!--  Question  --> 
As of yet, 
however, 
not much is known about 
eHUBS with on-site recharging of micro-mobility vehicles. 
It is unclear how the return-to-origin (A-to-A) 
restriction might impact on users and useability/practicality.   
Nor is it clear what potential hub offerings 
might better meet community needs (including through expansion). 
There also appears to be only limited understandings about 
how best to communicate information about such a hub and how to use it. 

<!--  Answer  --> 
Research understandings about eHUBs 
appear to be at an early stage, 
for which many authors^[See, for example, @Bonoma:1984aa, @Benbasat:1987aa, @Eisenhardt:1989aa, @Meredith:1993aa, @ Cavaye:1996aa, @Darke:1998aa, @Stuart:2002aa, @Voss:2002aa and @Yin:2018ab.] 
suggest adopting an exploratory case research approach. 
Industrial-design-based approaches, 
including those well suited to transport research 
^[See @Coxon:2018aa, @Coxon:2021ab, @Gaitan:2021aa, @Napper:2021aa, @Pink:2021aa, @UK-Design-Council:0aa and others.], 
such variously adopting iterative, 
co-design and participatory,
and creative 
processes. 
As such, this paper reports the findings from 
workshops with 
members of the public 
and project stakeholders 
held in Letterkenny, Galway and Waterford 
to explore 
attitudes, needs and ideas 
as to how the ‘base’ shared e-mobility hub might be leveraged 
and enhanced so as to better meet each community’s transport and other needs. 
The cross-case comparisons 
reported in this paper 
might provide policy-makers, 
practitioners and researchers 
further insights into the types of offerings that might be provided 
at shared e-mobility hubs and other transport facilities 
in a variety of contexts (small town, secondary town centre, suburban locations etc.) 
so as to enhance sustainable mobility and community outcomes 
in future such transport facility developments.
